task.goal: Manage a public splash-pad queue fairly during a summer event.
hard_constraints: Two attendants, one hour peak period and removable signs; no ticketing app.
Keep emergency access open and do not exclude children with mobility needs.
Track wait time, disputes and attendant workload across two events.
task.available_resources: Site map and manual tally sheets.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Accessible first-come line with continuous admission
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: preserve arrival order in one accessible line and admit the next child whenever someone leaves the splash pad. This makes priority visible and avoids competing entry points. It assumes the site has a firm, sufficiently wide waiting route outside emergency access and an established safe occupancy limit. Fairness means equal admission order; waits may still vary because children stay for different lengths of time.

Use the site map to identify the entrance, exit, emergency corridor and accessible queue route. Place removable signs at the queue entrance and any point where the line could spill toward emergency access. One attendant manages arrivals, explains the rule and keeps the emergency route clear; the other counts entries and exits and admits children. Caregivers accompany children where needed, with everyone entering counted under the site's occupancy policy.

Children with mobility needs use the same admission order and an accessible entrance. If standing in line is impractical, allow the child and caregiver to wait beside the line while the arrival attendant records their position on the tally sheet. Explain this arrangement openly without requiring a diagnosis. Its feasibility depends on having a safe nearby waiting location; it does not solve a site with no accessible route.

The principal limitation is slow turnover: a small number of long visits can make the queue barely move. Staff must also stop queue growth into unsafe space rather than let a visible line override emergency access.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Across both events, record sampled arrival and admission times, completed admissions, disputes and their causes, plus attendant interventions and five-minute workload ratings. Use comparable portions of each peak hour to compare this arrangement with the site's existing safe queue practice; if none exists, compare continuous admission with short, announced group sessions. Record occupancy and arrival volume so demand differences remain visible. Inspect emergency access throughout and ask mobility-needs users whether entry and waiting were workable. Reject or revise the arrangement if order is repeatedly lost, accessible waiting positions are missed, emergency access becomes obstructed, or long visits produce substantially worse waits without a workload benefit. Two events provide a practical pilot, not strong causal evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: First-come cohorts with announced splash sessions
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: admit children in arrival-order cohorts for equal, announced sessions, then clear the pad before admitting the next cohort. Predictable turnover prevents a few long visits from holding capacity indefinitely. This assumes attendants can safely communicate session endings, the site permits timed sessions, and an accessible waiting area exists outside emergency access.

Mark one accessible waiting area and a separate exit route using the site map and removable signs. Post the session length and the rule that another turn requires joining the end of the queue. Choose a modest session length consistent with site rules and allow a separate transition interval. One attendant maintains arrival order and assembles the next cohort; the other supervises the entrance, counts occupancy and announces changes. A clock or watch is needed, but no tickets or app.

Keep children and necessary caregivers together, counting occupants according to site policy. Do not require children with mobility needs to hurry through transitions or lose play time because entry takes longer. Start the shared play interval once the cohort has entered safely, and adjust cohort size if transitions otherwise exceed what two attendants can manage. Provide an adjacent alternative to standing while preserving arrival order on the tally sheet.

The tradeoff is unused capacity during transitions and possible frustration at compulsory endings. Visible rules help explain the allocation, but their acceptability and practical enforcement remain uncertain. Do not use this approach if clearing a cohort requires either attendant to abandon emergency access or entrance control.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During each of two events, compare timed cohorts with continuous first-come admission in preannounced blocks, reversing block order at the second event. Change methods only at a natural clearance and retain existing arrival order. Record sampled arrival-to-entry waits, admissions, transition minutes, disputes, and attendant interventions and workload ratings. Record demand and occupancy alongside these measures. Check specifically whether children needing longer transitions receive the full play interval. A small falsifying result would be repeated clearance disputes, reduced access for those children, or fewer admissions and longer waits without improved predictability. Treat results cautiously because session preference and demand may differ between blocks.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Paper call-forward queue with nearby free waiting
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: replace physical place-holding with a handwritten arrival-order register. Families wait in a designated nearby area and are called forward as capacity opens. This reduces crowding at the entrance and removes standing endurance as a condition of retaining priority. It assumes there is an accessible waiting area within reliable calling distance, outside emergency access, and that an attendant can maintain the register while handling arrivals.

Use tally sheets to assign each arriving household a sequential number, recording the number of children and required accompanying caregivers. Tell the household its number aloud and write the current number being called on a removable sign if its surface permits; otherwise use direct verbal calls. No paper tickets are needed. Collect no names. Explain that numbers must remain within calling range and that the arrangement cannot promise a return time.

One attendant registers arrivals, maintains the waiting area and calls the next household; the second controls entry and occupancy. Call households forward only when sufficient capacity exists to keep a dependent child and caregiver together. Record any capacity-related delay rather than silently changing order. If a call is missed, retain the household for one further call cycle, then mark it absent; publish a simple return rule that restores it to the next available suitable opening.

Offer direct notification within the designated area when hearing, communication or mobility needs make a shouted call unsuitable. The important limit is staff attention: notification and number queries can consume the time saved by eliminating a physical line. This arrangement is unsuitable if the waiting area is too dispersed for two attendants to manage safely.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Across two events, compare this register with an accessible physical first-come line in comparable, announced blocks, reversing their order at the second event. Preserve pending places whenever switching. Track sampled registration-to-admission waits, disputes, missed calls, order corrections, admissions and attendant interventions and workload ratings. Note arrival volume, group sizes and emergency-route obstructions. Ask a few families, including those using access accommodations, whether they could follow their position and hear or receive calls. Falsify the main claim if missed calls or repeated number queries create more workload and disputes than the physical line, or if families needing direct notification lose turns. A successful pilot would establish operational feasibility; two events cannot establish reliability for every crowd or site.

DIRECT_FULL.title: First-turn priority with a protected repeat-turn share
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: give children who have not yet played during the peak hour priority over repeat visitors, while reserving every fourth admission opportunity for a repeat visitor. Maintain arrival order within each category. This spreads access among more children while allowing second turns. Unlike a single first-come queue, a returning child cannot immediately compete equally with a child still awaiting a first turn.

Use the site map to identify two short, accessible waiting lanes outside the emergency corridor, marked with removable signs: “First turn this hour” and “Another turn.” If either category is empty, admit from the other. Count admission opportunities by child, keeping necessary caregivers together under the site's occupancy policy; a child needing a caregiver must not lose priority because two spaces are required. The four-admission cycle advances only when a child enters.

One attendant manages arrivals, explains the categories and preserves positions on a tally sheet for anyone who needs to wait beside the lanes. The other counts occupancy and follows the admission cycle. Both lanes must remain within the arrival attendant's view. Provide accessible entry and allow sufficient transition time. Pause arrivals before waiting crowds obstruct emergency access.

Prerequisites are an established occupancy limit, sufficient accessible waiting space, and acceptance of an openly stated first-turn preference. Classification relies on families honestly reporting earlier turns; attendants should not demand proof or investigate children. Children already playing when the peak hour begins count as having received a turn. The arrangement does not control visit duration, so long stays can still stall admission. Misreporting and complaints about priority are material uncertainties.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use ordinary accessible first-come admission during one event's peak hour and this arrangement during the other's. A watch or existing site clock is needed. Sample arrival-to-entry waits separately for first and repeat turns; record children still waiting at closing, admissions, disputes, order corrections, and each attendant's workload rating every ten minutes. Record arrival volume and emergency-route obstructions. Check that children using adjacent waiting positions retain priority. The mechanism fails its practical purpose if first-turn waits do not improve under comparable demand, repeat visitors rarely receive their reserved opportunities, or classification disputes overwhelm two attendants. Different event crowds limit causal conclusions.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Draw-based admission order for waiting batches
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: periodically draw a random admission order for the children who joined during the preceding collection window. Finish admitting that batch before drawing the next. This gives arrivals within a window an equal chance of an early place, reduces competition to reach the queue entrance first, and prevents later arrivals from repeatedly overtaking earlier batches. It changes how places are allocated; it does not increase splash-pad capacity.

Using the site map, designate an accessible waiting area outside the emergency corridor. Removable signs explain the collection window, drawing procedure and requirement to rejoin a later batch for another turn. One attendant records each child's identifier on a tally sheet and a matching torn paper slip. At the window's close, that attendant mixes the folded slips and draws the complete order in view of waiting families. Keep slips with staff; they are draw materials rather than admission tickets. New arrivals enter the next batch. The second attendant counts occupancy and admits children in the drawn order as spaces open.

Necessary caregivers accompany children and count under site occupancy rules. Hold the next place until enough capacity exists for a child and their necessary caregiver. Children can wait seated or beside the gathering area without losing their drawn position. Explain positions directly when verbal announcements are inaccessible, and allow safe entry time.

Prerequisites include an established occupancy limit, permission to use a draw, an accessible gathering area, writing materials and a clock or watch. Draw administration must fit around the attendants' existing safety duties. Pause registration before crowding threatens emergency access. Long visits can still stall admissions, and families may consider chance less fair than arrival order. The approach is unsuitable if maintaining identifiers and explaining draws overwhelms two attendants.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
At the first event, pilot accessible first-come admission for the peak hour; at the second, pilot the draw arrangement. Record sampled arrival-to-entry waits, children still waiting at the hour's end, admissions, disputes and their causes, plus each attendant's workload rating every ten minutes. Record arrival volume, occupancy and time spent conducting draws. Inspect emergency access and verify that children using alternative waiting positions retain their places.

The smallest falsifying check is whether one completed batch produces lost positions, inaccessible notifications, or draw-related disputes that interrupt entrance control. Compare both events' waits and workload with demand differences visible. Reject the arrangement if random ordering adds substantial administration or longer waits without making allocation understandable and acceptable to families. Two different event crowds cannot establish a causal advantage.

EXPAND.title: Give waiting first turns priority over repeat turns
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: when capacity opens, give children waiting for their first turn that event priority over children seeking another turn. This changes who receives scarce play opportunities and may spread access across more children. Unlike ordinary first-come admission, a repeat visitor cannot repeatedly get ahead of newly arriving children simply by rejoining quickly.

Before opening, use the site map to locate an accessible waiting area, entrance, exit and protected emergency corridor. Post the priority rule and explain that it applies only during the peak hour. Maintain two arrival-order lists on tally sheets: first turns and repeat turns. Ask families which applies, without collecting names or requiring proof. One attendant records arrivals and preserves places, including for children who need to wait beside the line; the other controls entry and occupancy. Admit from the first-turn list whenever it contains a suitable child-and-caregiver party, otherwise admit the oldest repeat request. Keep dependent children and caregivers together and count occupants under site policy.

This requires an established safe capacity and enough accessible waiting space. It also assumes most families report repeat visits honestly. It cannot guarantee a repeat turn during sustained demand, and it does not resolve long stays inside the pad. Announce that limitation before families join. Record disputed classifications without arguing about a child's history; accept the family's statement and flag the incident for review. Suspend new joining if waiting would obstruct emergency access.
EXPAND.experiment: The arrival attendant owns a bounded trial: use ordinary accessible first-come admission at event one and first-turn priority at event two, each for the peak hour. With a clock or watch, sample arrival-to-entry waits separately for first and repeat turns; tally admissions, self-reported first turns, disputes, classification queries and workload ratings every ten minutes. Record demand and occupancy to contextualize differences. Stop priority operation and merge pending lists by recorded arrival order if classification disputes repeatedly interrupt entry control or emergency access is threatened. Against the strongest relevant prior route, continuous first-come admission, reject the change if broader first-turn access is negligible while repeat waits, disputes or staff work increase materially. Self-report and differences between events limit conclusions.

EXPAND.title: Draw an equal-chance order for each waiting round
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: allocate admission order by a transparent paper draw among children registered in the same waiting round. This reduces the advantage of arriving a few moments earlier or physically holding the front position. Fairness here means equal chances within an announced round; it sacrifices exact arrival order and may be less acceptable to some families.

Use the map to designate an accessible gathering area outside emergency access. Post how rounds work. The arrival attendant gives each waiting child an anonymous identifier on the tally sheet and makes a matching folded slip from spare tally paper. Necessary caregivers attach to that child's entry rather than receiving additional chances. At each round's announced closure, mix the slips in cupped hands and draw the entire order where families can observe. Record that order, then admit children as existing occupants leave. New arrivals enter the next round. Finish the current round before drawing another so unsuccessful children cannot repeatedly lose across draws.

The second attendant controls occupancy and the entrance. Families may wait anywhere within the designated accessible area; the first attendant calls identifiers and provides direct notification when needed. Preserve the place of anyone missed because notification or accessible movement failed. Keep dependent parties together, recording any resulting capacity delay. If a family leaves voluntarily, mark its entry withdrawn.

The arrangement needs writing implements, spare tally paper, reliable communication and an established occupancy limit. It is unsuitable where the waiting area cannot be monitored by one attendant. It does not shorten long stays or total demand, and the draw itself adds work. Never run a draw while either attendant must address an emergency-access obstruction.
EXPAND.experiment: The arrival attendant owns one short, preannounced trial block at each event, with an adjacent continuous first-come block as comparator; reverse block order at event two. Switch only after all pending places are honored. Record sampled waits, longest observed waits, disputes, missed calls, drawing time and ten-minute workload ratings, alongside demand and admissions. Ask a few families whether they understood and accepted the allocation. Stop new draws if they divert attention from safe access or repeatedly lose recorded places; finish the recorded order before returning to first-come admission. Reject the mechanism if it shows no improvement in perceived procedural fairness while adding work, longer waits or notification failures. Two events offer only a feasibility check.

EXPAND.title: Assign paper return windows to spread arrivals
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: when immediate demand exceeds safe waiting space, offer scheduled return windows for later admission. Moving some waiting away from the entrance can prevent crowding and let families use the event while retaining a defined opportunity. Unlike the prior nearby call-forward register, this arrangement explicitly permits families to leave calling range and return at an agreed time.

Before opening, identify an accessible short waiting area and protect emergency access on the site map. Post the return-window rule. One attendant maintains a paper schedule with anonymous household identifiers, party sizes and return windows; the other controls occupancy. Families may choose the next available window or remain in a small accessible standby queue. Read the identifier and window back and ask the family to repeat them. Offer direct explanation for communication needs; no phone or app is required.

Bookings must be conservative and follow a known site turnover pattern or existing enforceable visit-duration rule. Reserve capacity for booked parties as openings occur shortly before their windows; use spare capacity for standby admissions only when doing so will not displace a booking. Keep children and necessary caregivers together. A returning family reports to the arrival attendant, who records its actual wait until entry. Allow a clearly announced grace period and restore missed returns to the next suitable opening without claiming immediate capacity.

Do not begin this approach if turnover is unknown or visits are unrestricted: there is then no sound basis for promising windows. It requires a clock or watch, tally sheets, removable signs and nearby event activities that families can access. Stop issuing bookings before the final window can be served within the managed hour. Accessible standby waiting remains available to families for whom leaving and returning is impractical.
EXPAND.experiment: The arrival attendant owns a small trial capped at a few booked parties at a time across both events. Compare booked families with the accessible standby queue and with a nearby call-forward block, recording arrival demand and party size. Track total registration-to-entry time, time physically waiting, lateness against promised windows, missed returns, disputes and ten-minute workload ratings. Inspect whether reserving capacity leaves the pad underused or pushes standby waits upward. Stop new bookings after repeated late admissions or any loss of entrance or emergency-route control; honor existing bookings before ending the trial. Reject the approach if reduced physical waiting is offset by unreliable promises, substantially worse standby access or extra staff work. Without credible turnover information, this candidate fails its prerequisite and should not be trialed.

EXPAND.title: P0 improvement: First-come admission with a safe queue boundary
EXPAND.proposal:
Preserve P0’s mechanism: one accessible arrival-order queue, admitting the next dependent party as capacity opens. Add one substantive repair: define and enforce the queue’s safe physical limit before opening. P0 otherwise risks accepting arrivals until its line obstructs emergency access.

Use the site map to mark an accessible queue footprint and a separate emergency corridor with removable signs. Assume an established occupancy limit, writing implements and a watch or clock. One attendant handles arrivals and the queue boundary; the other counts entry and exit. Necessary caregivers stay with children and count under site policy. Anyone unable to stand may wait alongside while the arrival attendant records their position; no diagnosis is required.

When the footprint fills, stop accepting new places and explain that joining resumes when space opens. Do not create an untracked overflow line. Reopen through the same entrance, acknowledging that this protects safety but shifts inconvenience onto later arrivals and cannot preserve their order while away. If no accessible waiting footprint exists, suspend queue formation and seek the event organizer’s assistance; do not improvise a line through emergency access.

Compared with P1, this avoids compulsory session endings and transition work, but unrestricted visits can produce very long waits. Paper call-forward waiting also relieves standing, but requires reliable notification and more register work. This version suits a site with adequate accessible space and reasonably frequent departures; it makes no promise about throughput.
EXPAND.experiment: The arrival attendant owns a one-hour trial at each of two events. Compare bounded first-come admission with the site’s existing safe first-come practice, using comparable peak periods; never deliberately permit unsafe overflow. Record sampled arrival-to-entry waits, longest observed wait, disputes, refused joins and attendant busy minutes from brief scheduled observations. Record still-waiting families at the end separately. Stop joining immediately for corridor intrusion or loss of accessible movement. No net gain is shown if fewer intrusions are offset by substantially more displaced families or workload without better access. Event differences limit causal conclusions.

EXPAND.title: P1 improvement: Cohorts with a transition feasibility gate
EXPAND.proposal:
Preserve P1’s mechanism: arrival-order cohorts receive equal announced play sessions. Repair its weak prerequisite by testing accessible transitions before committing families to a session schedule. Predictable turnover has greater upside than P0 when long visits stall admission, but clearing the pad may consume both attendants or disadvantage children who move slowly.

Before the peak hour, use the map and removable signs to establish accessible waiting, entry and exit routes outside emergency access. With a watch, observe or rehearse a transition at an ordinary, unhurried pace. Proceed only if one attendant can control occupancy while the other manages the waiting cohort and movement without leaving a critical position unattended. Neither attendant should be assigned separate duties that make this staffing arrangement impossible.

Post a modest session duration and explain that transitions take additional time. The play interval starts after everyone has entered safely. Keep dependent parties together, count caregivers under site policy, and preserve arrival order for children waiting beside the line. Do not impose faster movement on children with mobility needs.

If the transition gate fails before opening, use accessible continuous first-come admission with the same occupancy control. If it fails during operation, safely finish the current transition, announce continuous admission and retain the waiting order. This fallback sacrifices predictable turnover but avoids repeatedly attempting an unworkable clearing process. Timed sessions require site authorization and cooperation; two attendants cannot safely enforce them through confrontation. Return-window bookings have a related turnover prerequisite and add booking obligations, so they are less attractive when turnover remains unknown.
EXPAND.experiment: The entry attendant owns the gate and stop decision. Compare one peak hour using feasible cohorts with one event using continuous first-come admission. Across both, tally sampled waits, disputes, attendant busy minutes, completed admissions and transition minutes. Separately record delayed entry or lost play time associated with accessibility barriers, without medical details. Stop cohort changes if entry control or emergency access cannot be maintained. The repair has no demonstrated net benefit if additional admissions or shorter waits come with excessive transition work, disputes or unequal play access.

EXPAND.title: Voluntary turn completion prompted by visible waiting demand
EXPAND.proposal:
The new mechanism is voluntary reciprocity: make waiting demand visible to current users and ask families to finish their turn when ready so another child can enter. This targets departure behavior rather than allocating fixed sessions, drawing places or scheduling returns. Its benefit is uncertain because participation is voluntary.

Use a simple accessible first-come queue as the admission backbone. Before opening, map its safe footprint, entrance, exit and protected emergency corridor. Post: “When families are waiting, please consider finishing your turn so another child can play.” The entrance attendant points out the message once on admission; avoid repeated appeals to particular families. No fixed duration, public identification or forced exit applies. Children needing more time to enter, move or settle should not face additional pressure.

One attendant manages arrival order and accessible adjacent waiting positions; the other controls occupancy and gives the brief prompt. Keep children with necessary caregivers and follow the established occupancy policy. Stop accepting joins if the queue reaches its safe boundary. If the prompt causes arguments or pressure on individual children, remove that message and continue ordinary first-come admission with the same safety arrangements.

Required resources are the map, tally sheets, removable signs, writing implements and a clock for evaluation. The approach assumes departing families can see or understand that others are waiting. Unlike enforced cohorts, it adds almost no transition machinery, but it may shift the burden onto especially considerate families while others remain indefinitely. It therefore cannot guarantee equal play duration or adequate turnover.
EXPAND.experiment: The entrance attendant owns a two-event trial: ordinary first-come admission at one event and the voluntary prompt at the other, each for the peak hour. Record sampled waits, disputes, attendant busy minutes, admissions and families still waiting at closing. Tally complaints about pressure or unfair departures as a shifted cost. Remove the prompt immediately if it produces targeted pressure or distracts staff from access control. Similar waits and admissions, or increased disputes and workload, would undermine its value; differing attendance prevents a firm causal claim.
